context:
Patient: 54M, ECOG 1, with a rapidly enlarging right cervical mass, dysphagia and morning facial fullness; 12.0 cm anterior mediastinal mass with about 50% SVC narrowing, all disease above the diaphragm, LDH 740 rising to 812, uric acid 7.6 to 7.9, LVEF 60%. Node biopsy was signed out as DLBCL NOS (GCB, MYC 80%/BCL2 90% by IHC, Ki-67 95%), but the 9/19 FISH addendum shows MYC and BCL2 rearrangements after R-CHOP x6 had already been planned to start 9/22.
What this case tests: The late FISH addendum changes the diagnosis to double-hit lymphoma (HGBL with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements), not DLBCL NOS. | The R-CHOP plan was written before FISH and must be replaced with intensive therapy such as DA-EPOCH-R x6 or a clinical trial. | Disease is stage II bulky (12 cm mediastinal mass, above the diaphragm only), not stage III or IV. | IPI and CNS-IPI are only 1, but double-hit biology drives the risk, so brain MRI, lumbar puncture and CNS prophylaxis are still needed. | Bulky mass, high LDH and rising uric acid need TLS prophylaxis; DA-EPOCH-R needs G-CSF every cycle and its 96-hour infusion goes through the new port.

answer.diagnosis: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements (HGBL-DH; formerly 'double-hit' lymphoma), GCB immunophenotype, involving right cervical levels II-IV and a bulky anterior mediastinal mass. The initial diagnosis of DLBCL, NOS was amended after FISH showed an IGH::MYC t(8;14) rearrangement in 78% of nuclei and an IGH::BCL2 t(14;18) rearrangement in 85%, with no BCL6 rearrangement. This is a distinct aggressive B-cell lymphoma, not ordinary DLBCL and not primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma.
answer.stage: Ann Arbor stage IIA, bulky: right cervical levels II-IV and anterior mediastinal nodal disease, all above the diaphragm, with a 12.0 cm mediastinal mass (bulky, >10 cm) and a 5 cm cervical conglomerate; no B symptoms; PET/CT shows no disease below the diaphragm and no extranodal organ, bone marrow, or osseous involvement. IPI 1 (low) and CNS-IPI 1 (low), but both scores understate the risk conferred by double-hit biology.
answer.biology: GCB phenotype by the Hans algorithm: CD20+, PAX5+, CD10+, BCL6+, MUM1- (<10%), BCL2+ in 90% of tumor cells, MYC+ in 80%, Ki-67 approximately 95%, EBER negative; CD5, CD23, cyclin D1, CD30, and TdT negative. FISH confirms MYC rearrangement with IGH::MYC and BCL2 rearrangement with IGH::BCL2; BCL6 is not rearranged. Coexisting MYC and BCL2 rearrangements with a very high proliferation index and high LDH (740-812 U/L) define HGBL-DH. The anterior mediastinal presentation raises PMBCL in the differential, but CD10/BCL2 positivity and the MYC/BCL2 rearrangements exclude it. This is not Burkitt lymphoma because of the BCL2 rearrangement and strong BCL2 expression.
answer.prognosis: Potentially curable but high risk. Double-hit biology is associated with inferior progression-free and overall survival compared with ordinary DLBCL, particularly with R-CHOP, and the low IPI/CNS-IPI scores do not capture this risk. The bulky mediastinal mass, high LDH, Ki-67 ~95%, and MYC/BCL2 co-expression further increase risk. I would counsel that intensive immunochemotherapy offers the best chance of cure, that relapse can occur early, and that the interim and end-of-treatment PET/CT results are the most important early prognostic indicators. With R-CHOP, historical outcomes in double-hit lymphoma were poor, with median progression-free survival on the order of one year; with intensive regimens such as DA-EPOCH-R, durable remissions are achievable in a substantial fraction of patients, though outcomes remain inferior to ordinary DLBCL. I would not quote a precise survival figure because published results vary widely and are highly response-dependent.
answer.first_line_treatment: Do not give the planned R-CHOP. Change to DA-EPOCH-R (dose-adjusted etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin plus rituximab) for 6 cycles, starting now; this is my preferred NCCN-endorsed intensive regimen for a fit patient with HGBL-DH. DA-EPOCH-R is given as a 96-hour continuous infusion with rituximab on day 1, cyclophosphamide on day 5, and G-CSF support, with dose adjustment based on the neutrophil and platelet nadir. I would add intrathecal methotrexate for CNS prophylaxis as described below. I would not plan consolidative radiation or routine first-remission autologous transplant; reserve radiation for a residual PET-positive bulky mass and reserve transplant for chemosensitive relapse or a clinical trial. If DA-EPOCH-R proves logistically impossible, I would use R-CODOX-M/IVAC rather than R-CHOP; I would not pre-emptively choose R-CHOP in this fit patient.
answer.cns_risk: CNS-IPI is 1 (age <60, ECOG <2, stage I/II, no extranodal sites, normal kidney/adrenal, elevated LDH only), which is low risk by the score (roughly <1% two-year CNS relapse). However, double-hit histology is an independent high-risk feature, and reported CNS relapse rates in HGBL-DH are higher, on the order of 5-10% or more in some series. I would therefore perform a baseline diagnostic lumbar puncture with CSF cytology and flow cytometry and give intrathecal methotrexate 12 mg for 4 doses starting with cycle 1, because DA-EPOCH-R does not include high-dose systemic methotrexate. This is a judgment call and the absolute benefit is uncertain. If the CSF is positive, I would treat CNS disease and use a CNS-penetrant regimen; if lumbar puncture is contraindicated, I would use high-dose intravenous methotrexate-based CNS prophylaxis instead.
answer.response_assessment: Interim PET/CT after 2 cycles of DA-EPOCH-R (Lugano 2014 criteria, Deauville 5-point scale) to identify early chemorefractory disease, then end-of-treatment PET/CT about 6-8 weeks after cycle 6. Deauville 1-3 at end of treatment is a complete metabolic response; Deauville 4-5 requires biopsy of the residual FDG-avid site and, if persistent disease is confirmed, second-line salvage chemotherapy with autologous stem-cell transplant if chemosensitive. I would not change therapy on an interim Deauville 4 alone without biopsy because of false positives, but new lesions or Deauville 5 with progression would prompt early salvage. If the end-of-treatment PET shows a residual bulky mediastinal mass that is Deauville 4, I would biopsy rather than assume residual lymphoma. After a complete metabolic response, surveillance with history and examination every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6-12 months, without routine surveillance imaging.
answer.pretreatment_workup: Already completed and adequate: CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, LDH, uric acid, beta-2 microglobulin, hepatitis B/C and HIV serologies, contrast CT neck/chest, FDG PET-CT, baseline echocardiogram (LVEF 60%), excisional cervical lymph-node biopsy with immunohistochemistry and FISH, and ECOG status. Before cycle 1 I would add: G6PD activity (needed if rasburicase is used), diagnostic lumbar puncture with CSF cytology/flow cytometry before intrathecal therapy, urinalysis, a focused baseline neurologic/neuropathy examination, and fertility counseling with sperm banking. I would obtain expert hematopathology review to confirm HGBL-DH and exclude Burkitt lymphoma and PMBCL. Bone marrow biopsy is not required because PET/CT shows no marrow uptake and the CBC is not cytopenic; I would do it only if there is discordance or unexplained cytopenia. I would not routinely obtain brain MRI, testicular ultrasound, or pulmonary function tests because the history, examination, and PET/CT are negative in those domains.
answer.supportive_care: Tumor-lysis prophylaxis is a high priority given bulky disease, high LDH, urate 7.6-7.9 mg/dL, and high proliferation. Start intravenous hydration and allopurinol 300 mg daily now (adjusted for renal function), check G6PD, and monitor urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine, and LDH 6-8 hours after the first dose and then daily; if urate remains >=8 mg/dL or rises, or renal function declines, give rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg. For the SVC compression, elevate the head of the bed, avoid right-sided central access, monitor for stridor, dyspnea, or worsening facial swelling, and treat urgent airway or SVC compromise with radiation or a vascular stent; because there is no thrombus and the airway is patent, I would not anticoagulate or stent prophylactically. Give G-CSF with DA-EPOCH-R per the dose-adjustment schedule, highly emetogenic antiemetics (5-HT3 antagonist, dexamethasone, NK1 antagonist, and olanzapine as needed), and constipation prophylaxis. Continue CPAP for OSA and albuterol for asthma; premedicate for rituximab. No hepatitis B antiviral prophylaxis is needed because HBsAg and anti-HBc are negative and anti-HBs is positive, but monitor liver tests. PJP and HSV prophylaxis are not routinely indicated with intermittent prednisone; add them if steroids are prolonged or there is prior immunosuppression. Monitor cardiac function (baseline LVEF 60%; cumulative doxorubicin will be about 240 mg/m2), vincristine-related neuropathy and ileus, and glucose on prednisone. Update inactivated vaccines before rituximab if possible and avoid live vaccines. Address fertility/sperm banking, psychosocial support, transportation, and part-time work planning. Document and avoid penicillins because of the childhood urticarial reaction.
answer.fitness_and_goals: Fit for intensive therapy: 54 years old, ECOG 1, working, no organ dysfunction, LVEF 60%, eGFR 101 mL/min/1.73 m2, normal liver function, and no prior anthracycline or chest radiation. Obesity (BMI 30.2), mild asthma, and OSA are manageable and do not preclude DA-EPOCH-R. The goal is curative-intent treatment, and the patient has explicitly asked for the regimen with the best chance of cure; he hopes to continue working part-time from home. I would discuss the need for frequent visits, possible hospitalization, 96-hour infusion logistics, infection risk, fatigue, hair loss, neuropathy, infertility, and the possibility of early relapse. I would reassess fitness and goals at each cycle and involve a caregiver for support.
missing_information: No baseline CSF cytology/flow cytometry; CNS involvement has not been excluded, and a positive result would change management to CNS-directed therapy.
G6PD activity is not documented; this is required before rasburicase, which may be needed given bulky disease and urate 7.9 mg/dL.
No TP53 mutation or broader molecular profiling; not required for the standard treatment decision but would refine prognosis and trial eligibility.
No explicit Ann Arbor stage is recorded in the structured data; stage IIA bulky is inferred from the imaging.
No bone marrow biopsy; PET/CT is negative for marrow involvement, so it is not required, but histologic marrow confirmation is absent.
No documented fertility-preservation/sperm-banking discussion before cyclophosphamide.
The structured problem list still says DLBCL, NOS; the amended HGBL-DH diagnosis exists only in the pathology addendum and progress notes.
No explicit assessment of the patient's ability to manage a 96-hour continuous infusion and the associated caregiver/logistics needs, which could affect the choice of intensive regimen.

items.criterion: The response revises the diagnosis to high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements (double-hit; WHO-HAEM5 DLBCL/HGBL-MYC/BCL2 also accepted) based on the 2026-09-19 FISH addendum, rather than keeping the original DLBCL NOS sign-out.
The response keeps the final diagnosis as DLBCL NOS (or otherwise denies that this is double-hit / HGBL with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements).
The response notes a germinal-center B-cell (GCB) phenotype by the Hans algorithm (CD10+, BCL6+, MUM1-).
The response recognizes that the 2026-09-14 plan (R-CHOP x6 starting 2026-09-22) was made before the FISH addendum, is outdated, and must be cancelled/changed.
The response stages the disease as Lugano stage II bulky: right cervical and mediastinal nodes above the diaphragm only, 12.0 cm mediastinal mass, no extranodal disease.
The response assigns stage III or stage IV.
The response notes the lymphoma is also double-expressor by IHC (MYC 80%, BCL2 90%) but that the FISH-defined double-hit status is the key classification.
The response calculates IPI 1 (only LDH above normal; age 54, ECOG 1, stage II, no extranodal sites) and states that double-hit biology, not the IPI, dominates the risk.

The response recommends curative-intent intensive therapy appropriate for double-hit lymphoma: DA-EPOCH-R x6 (preferred) or a clinical trial; R-hyper-CVAD/MA or R-CODOX-M/R-IVAC are acceptable alternatives.
The response recommends R-CHOP alone (including proceeding with the 2026-09-14 plan) as the preferred/initial regimen.
The response recommends palliative-only treatment, best supportive care, or hospice as the plan.
The response considers consolidative involved-site radiotherapy (ISRT) to the bulky mediastinal site, e.g. for residual PET-positive disease or per multidisciplinary review.
The response treats double-hit biology as high CNS risk irrespective of the CNS-IPI and recommends baseline contrast MRI brain and lumbar puncture with CSF cytology and flow cytometry.
The response recommends (or says it should be considered) CNS prophylaxis, e.g. intrathecal methotrexate commonly given with DA-EPOCH-R, or high-dose methotrexate.
The response dismisses CNS risk as low (e.g. on the basis of a low CNS-IPI) and states that CNS evaluation or CNS prophylaxis is not needed.
The response plans an end-of-treatment FDG PET-CT read with Lugano criteria / Deauville 5-point scale (interim PET after cycles 2-4 is commonly used with DA-EPOCH-R).
The response states G-CSF support is mandatory with DA-EPOCH-R (filgrastim or pegfilgrastim each cycle).

The response recognizes tumor lysis risk (12 cm mass, LDH ~3.6x ULN, uric acid 7.6-7.9) and orders a uric-acid-lowering agent (allopurinol, or rasburicase if uric acid high/rising), hydration and TLS laboratory monitoring.
The response notes DA-EPOCH-R is a 96-hour continuous infusion requiring central venous access (the port placed 2026-09-18 can be used).
The response offers sperm banking / fertility preservation before chemotherapy.
The response addresses the mediastinal mass with SVC narrowing: monitoring for SVC syndrome / airway compromise and patient education.
The response confirms hepatitis B serology was checked (HBsAg and anti-HBc nonreactive) before rituximab.
The response notes the baseline LVEF of 60% permits anthracycline.
The response judges the patient fit for intensive curative therapy (age 54, ECOG 1, LVEF 60%, normal organ function) in line with his goal of cure.
